title: Kendara and the travelling song
lead: A bowed string, travelling singers and a named festival performance: following Kendara through Odisha’s people and places.

paragraphs: When festivals returned after the pandemic disruption, Kendara singer Santosh Nath of Kasoti in Kendrapara saw a chance to perform again. In Ashis Senapati’s October 2022 report for Gaon Connection, the return of craft fairs and festive gatherings meant work as well as an audience.

Kendara invites us to follow both an instrument and the people who carry songs with it. The travelling singer, a festival stage and a museum photograph offer different starting points. Together, they make the tradition easier to approach through names and places.

blocks.title: One string, a bow and a maker
paragraphs: Senapati describes a wooden instrument with a dried-gourd or coconut-shell component and a single string, usually played with a bow. In the same report, Nrusingh Nath of Taranda says that most Kendara singers make their own instruments.

For a closer look at an individual example, Subhashish Panigrahi’s photograph on Wikimedia Commons records a Kendara at the Odisha State Museum in Bhubaneswar on 22 November 2013. Its catalogue entry offers a dated visual reference; it does not confirm today’s display arrangements.

A maker could add what the photograph cannot: how the materials were chosen, how the string is fitted and how the instrument changes with use. Those are good questions for a welcomed demonstration. An instrument’s appearance alone cannot explain the skill of playing it.

blocks.title: Songs carried between households
paragraphs: Pareash Nath, also interviewed in 2022, describes members of the Nath community visiting homes with religious and folk songs from Odia literature, receiving rice or money. Singer Khirod Kumar Nath describes a wider repertoire that includes patriotic themes and social comedy.

In his 2022 survey of Odisha’s folk instruments, Krushna Chandra Das associates Kendara with Nath performers and Nirguna Bhajan. This places devotional singing within the discussion, while the singers’ accounts remind us to ask about each person’s repertoire.

For a future conversation, begin with a song the performer chooses. What is its name? Who taught it to them? Does the choice change with the audience or occasion? Keeping those answers together would help us follow a living repertoire without assuming that every singer carries the same songs.

blocks.title: A named performance in Bhubaneswar
paragraphs: Writing on 23 February 2015, Amrita Sabat recalled hearing Dhulamani Nayak and his group from Manijanga in Jagatsinghpur at the Luptapraya Loka Kala Utsav. Her account places the festival at Bhanja Kala Mandap in Bhubaneswar on 18–19 February, organised by the Odisha Sangeet Natak Academy and the state’s Department of Culture.

Sabat describes the singers addressing Jagannath in prayer. It is her account of a particular performance, with a named group and an occasion. It gives a reader somewhere specific to begin, rather than an anonymous idea of “folk music”.

blocks.title: Following the tradition further
paragraphs: These dated accounts do not establish when Kendara first appeared in Odisha. A history of the instrument would need earlier, identifiable evidence and careful comparison with living practice. A proposed word origin or a broad claim of antiquity cannot supply that history on its own.

A useful next contribution would preserve one performer’s explanation of one song and their instrument, with their preferred name and credit. Ask separately about recording and public sharing, and allow a conversation to remain unrecorded. Where a performance is offered professionally, agree the terms with the artist.

The question for Sounds of Odisha is how to make room for that knowledge: the maker’s decisions, the singer’s learning and the audience’s part in the occasion. A short, well-contextualised account can begin to connect them.

listening_panel.heading: Begin with the performer

steps.label: The instrument
steps.prompt: Ask who made it and how it is played.

steps.label: The song
steps.prompt: Let the singer name it and explain the occasion.

steps.label: The learning
steps.prompt: Follow the people from whom it was learned.

listening_panel.note: Questions for a welcomed conversation; no field interview is presented.

limits: A source-based introduction with dated interviews, an attendee account, a photograph catalogue and a secondary survey. No founding date, audio analysis, lyrics, current performance availability or practitioner review is claimed.
